title: Alspach's Question (1981)
statement_text: Is the maximum perimeter gap (the gap between the circumference and the order of the digraph) a growing function of $n$ for connected vertex transitive digraphs on $n$ vertices?
context_text: Trotter and Erdős proved in 1978 that there are infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs which are not Hamiltonian, leaving open how long a directed cycle one can guarantee in a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices. Alspach asked in 1981 whether the perimeter gap is a growing function of $n$.
paper_contribution: Resolves the question in the affirmative, proving that the perimeter gap grows at least as fast as $(1-o(1))\ln n$, and establishes a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ on the circumference.
notes: Attributed to Alspach [1] (1981). The paper fully resolves this question.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: There exists an $\varepsilon>0$ and infinitely many values of $n$ for which there exists a connected vertex transitive digraph of order $n$, whose perimeter gap is at least $\varepsilon n$.
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Trotter and Erdős gave infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs with no Hamilton cycle, and Alspach asked in 1981 whether the perimeter gap of such digraphs can be arbitrarily large. The authors answer this: for infinitely many $n$ there is a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices (a Cartesian product of two directed cycles, a Cayley digraph of an abelian group) with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$; and they prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n\ge2$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ (and a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$), a directed analogue of Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound for vertex transitive graphs, the best undirected bound now being $\Omega(n^{9/14})$ (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan). Determining the best possible bounds seems far out of reach, since even the undirected case is not understood; the authors propose this conjecture as a more attainable intermediate target, and say that even improving their logarithmic lower bound on the perimeter gap to a polynomial one would be interesting.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: Let $c(n)$ denote the minimum circumference of a connected vertex transitive graph on $n$ vertices. Let $d(n)$ denote the minimum circumference of a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices. Then $d(n)=\Theta(c(n))$.
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Trotter and Erdős gave infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs with no Hamilton cycle, and Alspach asked in 1981 whether the perimeter gap of such digraphs can be arbitrarily large. The authors answer this: for infinitely many $n$ there is a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices (a Cartesian product of two directed cycles, a Cayley digraph of an abelian group) with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$; and they prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n\ge2$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ (and a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$), a directed analogue of Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound for vertex transitive graphs, the best undirected bound now being $\Omega(n^{9/14})$ (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan). Since an undirected graph is a special digraph, $d(n)\le c(n)$. The authors' $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ bound for digraphs is weaker than the best undirected bound, and they suggest at least matching it asymptotically, or even proving this conjecture that the directed and undirected answers are asymptotically the same. The undirected proofs do not extend because they rely on the fact that any two longest cycles of a 2-connected graph intersect, which fails badly for strongly 2-connected digraphs.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

title: Question 4.3
statement_text: Is it true that in any connected vertex transitive digraph, any two longest directed cycles intersect?
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Two cycles intersect if they share a vertex. In a 2-connected undirected graph any two longest cycles intersect, a fact used crucially in all proofs of long cycles in vertex transitive graphs (Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound and its improvements). This fails for strongly 2-connected digraphs: the authors give strongly 2-connected digraphs with all in- and out-degrees equal to 2 whose longest directed cycles have length four and which contain arbitrarily many vertex-disjoint longest cycles (while directed paths are arbitrarily long). They nevertheless prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$, and ask whether vertex transitivity is a condition that guarantees that longest cycles pairwise intersect, which would help translate undirected results to digraphs.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

title: Question 4.4
statement_text: Does there exist $C>0$ such that in any vertex transitive digraph, the length of a longest path is by at most a factor of $C$ larger than the length of a longest directed cycle?
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Paths and cycles are directed. In connected vertex transitive undirected graphs, the lengths of a longest path and of a longest cycle are within a constant factor of each other by a classical result. The authors prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices has a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ but only a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$; in general digraphs, even strongly 2-connected ones, long directed paths do not force long directed cycles. Their construction of connected vertex transitive digraphs with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$ shows that the two lengths can differ by at least an additive logarithmic term, since it is a Cayley digraph of an abelian group and such digraphs always have a directed Hamiltonian path (Holsztyński and Strube).
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs
